title: Part 4
text: generators got done. Let them power up. Let the gates open. Let them run . He just wanted to spear the saboteur through the eye socket with a jagged IV stand and maybe crush a few tiles for good measure. The Entity’s judgment was already burning in the back of his skull — sharp, electric. Her attention stung. Jake’s little stunt with the hook had tipped him further into Her disfavor, and he could feel the leash tightening. One kill. That’s all he needed. Just one — and She might let him breathe again. That was the calculus now. One guaranteed sacrifice to take the edge off the migraine of divine punishment clawing through his thoughts. He could manage that. And on a personal level? The audacity of these survivors was insulting. Hiding instead of playing. No flair. No drama. No fucking respect for the hunt anymore. What was the point of all this if they were just going to cower ? He doubled back to check on his prize, staring for a moment at the discarded handcuffs, empty and swinging gently from their spot on the cabinet. Of course the cop was gone. Of COURSE . He ground his teeth and clenched the baton in his fist hard enough that the current snapped along its length. Three guesses which pest had cut the leash. If he hadn’t diverted toward the last generator’s detonation, hoping to pick someone off mid-flee, he might’ve caught them. A rare lapse in judgment. One he wouldn’t make again. They only had one generator left. And now, all of them were in the same wing. A bottleneck. He could practically feel the survivors trying to creep their way back toward it. Perfect. With deliberate steps, he angled himself toward the final sector, threading through the halls like a wolf circling its cornered prey. This trial wasn’t over yet. And nobody — nobody — was getting out if he had anything to say about it. When Herman entered the central hallway linking the last of the generators, he didn’t expect a roadblock. Yet there Jake stood — centered, unmoving, arms stretched wide across the narrow space as if he were enough to stop a monster. It was such a stupid pose, so mockingly symbolic, that for a split second, Herman nearly burst out laughing. So. The pest was done running. This could be an easy takedown. No thrill, no chase — just a single, cathartic strike to vent his fury and be done with it. But something in his posture, in the look of his eyes, gave Herman pause. Not defiance. Resolve . Not the kind that shouted or bluffed or begged. The quiet kind. The suicidal kind. The kind Herman had seen in soldiers who stopped flinching once the worst outcome became acceptable. That... piqued his curiosity. He came to a stop, eyeing the young man curiously. "I want to make a deal." Well... this was new. Survivors often begged, pleaded, screamed at him to stop. Sometimes they even tried offering the items they brought through the Fog in appeasement. But attempting a bargain? The absurdity of it made Herman cock his head, eyes narrowing with a flicker of amusement. "Audacious, aren't we? What part of this makes you think you are in any position to be making demands ?" Jake fought back a shiver, took a breath to steel himself, prayed the Doctor didn't notice the light tremor in his hands betraying how hard he was working to stand still . “I’m going to help finish the last generator. The girls will leave through the gate unharmed. You’ll send Leon back to the campfire. Through the Entity.” A hook sacrifice. Specifically, the one he had originally been denied. The very same fate Jake had denied his teammate earlier, now offered up like a sacred ritual. Full circle. Poetic. It would be satisfying on principle alone — watching the guilt curdle behind his eyes as he undid his own moral stand — but more than that, it was useful . A hook kill guaranteed his offering. No complications. No escape attempts. No malfunctions. One solid sacrifice to ease the pressure in his skull. Still... He wasn’t in a rush to agree. "I see,” Herman’s tone dripped bitterness. “And what, pray tell, do you offer in exchange for such lavish generosity on my part?” Jake's face hardened. He lowered his arms, trying to straighten his posture, hoping he looked more confident than he felt. "Once the others safely gone, I'll let you send me back to the campfire however you want." A shiver of static surged down Herman’s spine, excitement flaring sharp and visceral before he could even mask it. He inhaled, slow and deliberate, and the charge built in his chest like a thunderhead. Electricity crackled along his arms, climbing his sleeves in visible arcs as it danced across his fingertips. Jake flinched. Just barely. But it was there. The offer had struck its target. A willing sacrifice. No hunt. No chase. No wasted effort on disarming or downing or dragging. Just four full minutes — four — of undisturbed access to a live, consenting subject before the Fog claimed its due. Oh, he could work with that. Now THIS . This was a bargain worth his attention. "If I agree to your terms, what guarantee do I have that you won't simply slip away the moment the gate opens?" Jake blinked, genuinely surprised it had gotten this far. “I mean... you don’t,” he admitted. “Just like I’ve got no guarantee you won’t just capture the others anyways and still kill me for the hell of it.” His mouth was dry, tongue sticking slightly to the roof of it. But he held his ground, forced himself not to waver. “I guess we’d both be taking it on faith.” Jake shifted and held out a hand, his eyes fiercely locked into the Doctor's manic stare, daring him. A dare. A challenge. A goddamn death sentence, sealed with eye contact and hope his guts didn’t betray him right there on the floor. Herman stared at the offered hand, weighting the situation. Survivors often couldn't be trusted, but this one held himself with the conviction of a man who knew full well what he was offering and still chose it. Fascinating. He breached the gap between them with barely a half step, locking Jake's outstretched hand in a crushing grip that sent sparks licking up his arm like a promise of things to come. Jake gasped through clenched teeth, but didn’t pull away. Good. Herman pulled him in slightly, enough for Jake to smell the sharp ozone on his breath, feel the faint tremor in the air around him from the static charge crawling through his veins. His voice lowered to a threatening growl as he towered over the smaller man. "Should you go back on your end of this, I will personally take every single one of your people who come through my domain. I will send them back to you broken and charred after slowly extracting every conscious thought they have ever had from their hollowed-out husk of a mind with my bare hands . Not a single one will be spared until I have taken what is owed to me. And every single one will return to the Fog with their last living thought being the knowledge that you did this to them. Are we clear?" Jake's defiant glare cracked ever so slightly, a sheen of terror passing over his eyes. He nodded briefly, and Herman felt the heartbeat under his grip quicken. Excellent . The fear would keep him honest. Besides, what he had planned was much more fun when the subject was trying to hold it together and failing beautifully. Deal accepted. Herman loomed at the far end of the hallway, keeping just enough distance that his terror radius wouldn’t bleed into the survivors’ ears. Close enough to monitor. Not close enough to break the illusion of choice . He wasn’t about to let Jake out of his sight. The man had proven himself a persistent thorn, and while Herman now had leverage, he wasn’t fool enough to underestimate desperation. If Jake decided to bolt, he’d be on him in a second. But for now, he watched. Jake and Claudette were hunched over the last generator, working in tandem, both trying to pretend that there wasn’t a killer watching their every move from the shadowed end of the corridor. Jake's relief was subtle but clear — he was glad Meg had gone for the gate. She wouldn’t have kept to the plan otherwise. Too stubborn. Too loud. Too righteous . He’d have sent both girls on ahead if he could have, but this was much faster with two. Even from his perch, Herman could see Jake’s shoulders trembling. Not from exhaustion — but from sheer effort. The restraint it took to stay put under this kind of pressure was commendable, in a way. A lesser man would’ve cracked already. He had sent the cop back first — Jake had led him back to their hiding place before circling back to the generator. He had put up no resistance, not after so much personalized attention, and only really showed any spark of consciousness when the hook went through him, letting out a quiet, pained sound and grabbing at the metal moments before the Entity's claws ran him through and took him for Her meal. Satisfying to watch, at the least, even if he didn't have enough in him to scream the way they usually do. Herman could feel the Entity's pressure ease up on his mind slightly at the offering as well, leaving him feeling much less strained. His quota wasn't quite there yet, but at least he wasn't at risk of receiving Her full attention for a while now. That was far more valuable to him right now. He needed Her to leave him be for a while. This one... was personal. Down the hall, the generator flared to life. Jake gave Claudette a firm, reassuring nod — go — and she didn’t hesitate. She slipped past him, creeping along the wall as she passed the Doctor, shrinking away from the slow, gleaming grin he offered her in return. At least someone in this trial had a healthy sense of fear. In the distance, rust screamed and metal groaned — sharp and strained under years of neglect — marking the gate’s slow, shuddering rise. The Fog shifted, its pressure subtly relaxing as the girls crossed the threshold. Gone. He sighed in mild annoyance, never liking to simply allow an escape. He had contemplated chasing them out, at least making them earn it before pulling back to watch them scramble across the threshold, but the collapse was a limited window and he didn't want to waste a second of it having to navigate back from the gate. Jake had already moved to the rotunda by the time Herman rejoined him, standing among the Entity's vein-like cracks that spread across the floor as the timer ticked down in their minds. The lights overhead cast a halo around him — arms curled tight around his chest, feet locked in place. It was nearly picture perfect, the way he stood there defiantly resisting the natural instinct to flee. Herman paused to admire the sight. The survivor hadn’t run. Hadn’t faltered. No tricks. No tantrum. He had actually meant it . Herman respected that. It would make this all the more rewarding. A wide grin peeled across his face as he stepped into the light, current dancing eagerly along his shoulders, snapping from nearby chairs like leashed lightning. His voltage was already rising — amped higher than it had been in months. Four minutes. More than enough. He raised a hand towards Jake, sparks licking across fingers with sharp, deliberate arches. “When you see Mr. Richter, do be sure to pass along my regards.” The lights flared — flooding the rotunda in an unnatural white — and somewhere, buried in the static and the sirens, a scream echoed through the walls. Chapter 8: Collateral Damage Jake slammed back into existence with a soundless scream, his lungs seizing around phantom fire. The air tore into him like barbed wire, too sharp, too dry, too fast — his mind stuttered around his senses in chaotic bursts of disorientation — uncoordinated limbs thrashing violently against the world around him. He clawed at his chest, the ground, whatever limbs or hands were near enough to catch. Anything to anchor himself. Anything to get out . Everything burned. His nerves lit up in jagged afterimages of torment, phantom electricity screaming down his spine and out through his limbs. No position gave relief. No movement lessened it. His mind stuttered and skidded across broken sensory input — sound and color and pressure flooding in all at once, none of it lining up, none of it making sense . A hundred fragments of reality all jammed into the same second. And something was touching him. Hands. Arms. Seemingly everywhere . Trying to hold him down. Voices, shouting, distant and warped like they were underwater. Jake erupted , flailing against the phantom restraints with every wild, adrenaline-drenched ounce of strength he had left. He couldn’t tell if he was hitting the floor or someone’s leg or a wall, but one of his fists caught something solid and some of the hands fell away, only to be replaced by even stronger ones. They hooked around his arms and shoulders, pulled him upright — someone braced behind him, locking him in place like a seatbelt. He had no balance, no leverage. His feet scrabbled uselessly across the ground. Everything was too much . Too loud, too bright. Light carved white-hot streaks across his vision. Sound hit in smeared vibrations, voices collapsing into meaningless noise. A scream caught in his throat as electricity still danced in phantom arcs along his spine. The arms locked across his chest didn’t budge — a steady pressure pinning him in place, anchoring him as he fought and flailed and finally... broke . Behind him, someone breathed slow and calm, exhaling soft rhythm into the crook of his neck, like trying to pace him down from the edge. A voice — low, familiar, more tone than any words he could recognize — murmured quiet nonsense against his ear. It didn’t matter what they were saying. The sound of it sliced through the screaming in his skull, dragging his mind back one fragile thread at a time. The fire in his chest slowed. The shaking dulled. Jake’s limbs sagged, twitching instead of thrashing, the force of his panic bleeding out in great gasping sobs that wracked his whole frame. His breath hitched again and again, caught between pain and grief and exhausted terror. The grip around him shifted, and he let it — let them pull him sideways, let his face be tucked against warm fabric and steady muscle, away from the worst of the light. The hands that had tried holding him down had softened into grounding touches and exploratory prods against pulse points and mostly healed burns. His mind swam. Ears roared. The adrenaline was gone but nothing coherent took its place — just static, floating somewhere below the surface of himself. He felt the world tip, just slightly, somewhere behind his ribs. His consciousness pitched downward, a wave folding in on itself — and Jake let it. Let it take him. Let the pain go. Let everything go. Soft murmurs stirred him back toward the surface — warm voices through the static, low and familiar. How long had he been out? Jake inhaled, wincing as the scent of burning wood and sweat flooded his senses. Campfire. Damp earth. Cloth soaked with adrenaline and blood. He blinked through the fog, squeezing his eyes shut against the light, body aching down to the bone. The camp. The other survivors. Safety . Pain still throbbed across his ribs, his arms, his spine — but it was distant now, dull. Already the Fog was doing its work, nibbling away at the worst of it. In a few trials, the memory of the pain would fade. Jake tried opening his eyes again and, through blurred static, caught on a blur of motion a short distance from the fire. Ace sat a little ways off, being gently interrogated by Dwight’s medkit. The man looked *rough *— one hell of a black eye blooming across his temple, sunglasses gone, and a shallow cut tracing just beneath his brow. He kept flinching as Dwight dabbed at him, muttering colorful commentary through the fussing. When he noticed Jake watching, Ace gave a crooked grin and a two-fingered salute — then winced again as Dwight swatted his hand away. Jake exhaled a weak breath that might’ve been a laugh if he had the energy. Right. That must’ve been who he hit. Something shifted against his back, and Jake glanced down to find a familiar scarred forearm wrapped around him, anchoring him to a battered shirt. David. He shifted slightly, only to realize he’d been curled against the man. Too tired to be embarrassed. Almost. Blinking away the haze, he spotted Claudette and Meg chatting quietly with Felix and Leon near the fire. Leon looked tired, his wrist tightly wrapped in layers of gauze. He was a little slouched in on himself, but alert, apparently in discussion over something. Meg caught his gaze and gave a tight smile. Jake let out a long breath and sagged against David’s side. They were OK. They made it out. “You back with us?” David’s voice was low and dry with a hint of amusement as he poked gently at Jake’s temple. Jake let out a weak chuckle, breath still shaky. “Think so?” He pushed himself upright, peeling away from the solid warmth of David’s chest with the sluggish reluctance of someone who very much would’ve preferred to stay there. He rubbed at his arms, trying to work life back into the aching muscles. “Little well done for my tastes,” he muttered, flexing his fingers experimentally, “but it feels like everything’s still attached.” He glanced across the firelight to where Leon sat, looking very much like he too could use a nap. “You good?” Leon nodded, voice a little hoarse. “Yeah. Don’t remember much after the girls came in, but I’m no worse for wear.” Good. That was good. If Leon was coherent, then it had been worth it. Jake exhaled and dropped his head again, letting the dizziness ebb out with the fire’s warmth. “Fuck,” he muttered, “that was way worse than his usual mori. My head’s still ringing.” David’s hand settled on his shoulder, keeping him from tipping over as the world kept pitching gently around his head. “Yeah, that tracks. Doctor gets creative sometimes. Bastard’s never satisfied just running the script.” Across the fire, Felix let out a soft snort — dry and humorless. “That’s an understatement,” he muttered, something unreadable flickering behind his eyes. “Just take your time. The aftershocks’ll pass, but you’re probably gonna have trouble holding anything for a bit.” Jake flexed his fingers again, watching as they twitched and jumped slightly in response. He may have to stay off gens for a little while, at least until he could hold the wires without his arms trying to choreograph random interpretive dance in the delicate machinery. He sat in silence for a while, letting the trembling slowly bleed out of his limbs while David traced slow, grounding circles over his back. Creative , he thought bitterly, really was a fucking understatement. He’d taken his fair share of electric shocks before — burned synapses, short-circuited thoughts, the usual Fog-induced brain scrambles. Painful, sure, but fast. Rote. Survivable. This had been something else entirely. He could still hear the crack of bones locking under their own tension. Still feel the collapsing pressure in his chest, every muscle turning against him with surgical precision. Still smell the sheer, unfiltered panic as his body refused to obey anything but the torment it was drowning in. He clenched his jaw and shoved it down. He was safe. The trial was over. His people were here. That was what mattered. The memory would fade from his nerves — eventually. The Fog would see to that, whether he liked it or not. But that lingering taste, the knowledge of what had been done? That wasn’t going anywhere. Just another piece of trauma to be shelved, right alongside all the others. Jake exhaled, letting his head rest on his knees. And yet, even with everything he was trying not to think about, one weird detail kept itching at the edge of his thoughts. “Hey, Felix?” Jake’s voice cut through the quiet, still scratchy but steady. “Why would the Doctor tell me to say hi to you for him?” Felix went rigid, his grin falling, replaced by a haunted vacancy that made Jake’s stomach twist. To one side, Jake felt David's posture stiffen slightly with a nearly silent inhale. Jake blinked. “What?” he asked cautiously. “What happened?” Felix didn’t answer. His breath hitched — almost a flinch — before he surged to his feet and stormed off into the darker edges of the camp, muttering something sharp and half-German under his breath. Meg and Leon watched him go; curiosity blended with sympathy clear in their eyes. Claudette chased after him, earning a heated string of words for her trouble that left her frozen at the treeline, helpless as he vanished into the woods. Several nearby survivors who’d been lingering too close scattered in his wake, ducking behind trees and cover like startled animals, fleeing the direct fire of the oncoming warpath. Jake started to rise, guilt sparking fresh adrenaline through his limbs — but David’s hand clamped around his wrist and pulled him back down. “What...? What did I do?” "Let him go,” David sighed softly. “Felix and the Doc... those two have history." Jake stared after the direction Felix had gone, brow furrowed. “The fuck did the Doctor do to him?” David shook his head, turning back to the fire, poking at the edge of the flames like they held better answers. “He doesn’t like to talk about it,” he said finally. “And I’m not about to do it for him. We all got our issues here. Let’s leave it at that.” A sudden crash rang out in the distance — something getting kicked over hard — and Jake winced, his nerves tightening in sympathy. Whatever had happened to Felix... it hadn’t faded with the Fog. It was clearly still very raw. David didn’t look up. “Gotta say though,” he muttered, flipping a smoldering branch. “If the Doc took time to stab at Felix before going after you... you’re lucky you came back in the state you did.” Jake stared into the fire, watching the flames dance in silence as the distant echo of German curses was swallowed by the Fog. A heavy quiet settled over the group — unsettling in its stillness. He’d thought the trial couldn’t have been worse. Couldn’t have hurt more. But now... now he wasn’t so sure. His nerves still trembled faintly beneath his skin. The air tasted sharp, gritty. His lungs stung when he drew a full breath. His bones felt hollowed out from the strain and shock, still aching in ways the Fog hadn’t soothed yet — and might not for a while. If this was lucky... Then what the hell did unlucky look like? His gaze drifted to the shadows where Felix had disappeared. What the hell had happened between him and the Doctor? Jake exhaled slowly, the fire’s warmth doing little to chase the chill settling in his gut. Hopefully, he’d never have to find out.
